dsa.sort-passes.title: Array state after k passes (selection, insertion, bubble)
dsa.sort-passes.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.sort-passes.check: Selection: pass i swaps the minimum of a[i:] into slot i (even if it is already there). Insertion: pass i inserts a[i] into the sorted prefix a[:i]. Bubble: pass p sweeps left to right and parks the p-th largest at the end; small items move left only one slot per pass.

dsa.sort-swaps.title: Counting swaps, shifts and comparisons
dsa.sort-swaps.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.sort-swaps.check: Bubble swaps = insertion shifts = number of inversions. Selection: always n(n-1)/2 comparisons and n-1 swap statements, some of them self-swaps. Insertion comparisons = shifts + (passes whose key stops before index 0). Early-exit bubble sort counts the final no-swap pass.

dsa.sort-props.title: Stability and best/worst cases of elementary sorts
dsa.sort-props.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.sort-props.check: Stable: insertion (strict >) and bubble (strict >). Unstable: selection (long-range swap). Best case Θ(n): insertion, early-exit bubble on sorted input. Selection is Θ(n²) always. Insertion = Θ(n + inversions); early-exit bubble passes = max leftward distance + 1.

dsa.sort-merge.title: Merge sort: merge comparisons, passes and properties
dsa.sort-merge.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.sort-merge.check: Merging runs of sizes m and n costs between min(m, n) and m + n - 1 comparisons; stop counting when one run empties. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n) on every input. Bottom-up pass k merges runs of size 2^(k-1).

dsa.sort-quick.title: Quicksort: Lomuto partition traces and cost
dsa.sort-quick.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.sort-quick.check: Lomuto (pivot a[hi]): i starts at lo-1; for each a[j] <= pivot do i += 1 and swap a[i], a[j] (a self-swap when i == j); finally swap a[i+1], a[hi]. One partition of k items makes k-1 comparisons. Sorted, reversed or all-equal input gives n-1 : 0 splits and Θ(n²).

dsa.dc-recur.title: Divide and conquer: recurrence to complexity
dsa.dc-recur.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.dc-recur.check: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a): smaller -> Θ(n^(log_b a)); equal (times log^k) -> multiply by one more log; larger (regular) -> Θ(f(n)). T(n) = T(n-1) + n is Θ(n²); T(n) = T(√n) + 1 is Θ(log log n).

dsa.graph-traverse.title: BFS and DFS visit order
dsa.graph-traverse.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.graph-traverse.check: BFS: FIFO queue, mark when enqueued, neighbours in the given order; whole level before the next. Recursive DFS: go to the first unvisited neighbour, backtrack only when none is left. A stack DFS that pushes neighbours in list order visits them in reverse order. Valid-order checks: BFS children of u come as a block; DFS may not leave a vertex that still has an unvisited neighbour.

dsa.graph-bfs-dist.title: BFS levels, unweighted shortest paths and components
dsa.graph-bfs-dist.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.graph-bfs-dist.check: BFS level = fewest edges from s; DFS depth is not a distance. Non-tree edges of a BFS tree join levels differing by at most 1. Count shortest paths level by level: paths(v) = sum of paths(u) over neighbours u one level up. Components: run BFS/DFS from every unvisited vertex; isolated vertices count; m >= n - k with equality iff forest.

dsa.graph-dfs-topo.title: DFS edge classification and topological sort
dsa.graph-dfs-topo.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.graph-dfs-topo.check: Directed DFS: tree edge to a new vertex; back edge to an ancestor still open (cycle); forward edge to an already finished descendant (d[u] < d[v]); cross edge to a finished vertex with d[v] < d[u]. Undirected DFS has only tree and back edges. Topological order = reverse finishing order, or Kahn: repeatedly remove an in-degree-0 vertex.

dsa.graph-dijkstra.title: Dijkstra trace and negative edges
dsa.graph-dijkstra.subject: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms
dsa.graph-dijkstra.check: Extract the unfinished vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relax its out-edges: d[v] = min(d[v], d[u] + w). A finalized vertex is never updated again, which is safe only when all weights are >= 0. A negative edge (even without a negative cycle) can make Dijkstra wrong; use Bellman-Ford.

```python
def selection_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n - 1):          # one pass per i
        m = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if a[j] < a[m]:
                m = j
        a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
```

```python
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key
```

In the same run (Lomuto quicksort on `[1, 2, ..., 9]`), how many swaps are executed in total if **every** execution of swap line 1 and swap line 2 counts, self-swaps included?

```python
def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]      # swap line 1 (runs even if i == j)
    a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]    # swap line 2
    return i + 1
```

options.text: Keys in descending order
options.why: The pivot is the minimum in the first call, so the split is 0 : n - 1; the descending structure keeps the splits lopsided.

options.text: All n keys equal
options.why: With `<=` every key goes left, so the pivot lands at hi and the split is n - 1 : 0 every time.

options.text: A uniformly random permutation (expected time)
options.why: Random input gives expected Θ(n log n); the bad cases need an adversarial or highly ordered input.

questions.solution:

2. Sorted, reversed and all-equal arrays all do this with a last-element pivot and `<=`.
3. Expected time on random input is Θ(n log n).

questions.stem: BFS is run from s on a connected, undirected, unweighted graph, giving levels d(v). Which statement is always true?

options.text: Every edge not in the BFS tree joins two vertices of the same level.
options.why: A non-tree edge can also join adjacent levels, e.g. a vertex with two parents one level up.

options.text: The depth of v in a DFS tree from s also equals d(v).
options.why: DFS can reach v by a long detour; only BFS depths are shortest distances.

options.text: BFS levels give shortest paths even when edges have different positive weights.
options.why: BFS counts edges, not weights; weighted graphs need Dijkstra.

options.text: For every edge (u, v) of the graph, |d(u) - d(v)| <= 1.
options.why: If d(v) were >= d(u) + 2, BFS would have reached v from u one level earlier.

questions.solution:
1. When u is dequeued, every unvisited neighbour gets level d(u) + 1.
2. So a neighbour of u has level at most d(u) + 1, and by symmetry |d(u) - d(v)| <= 1.

options.text: m >= n - k
options.why: Each component with c vertices needs at least c - 1 edges to be connected; summing gives n - k.

options.text: If m = n - k, the graph has no cycle.
options.why: Every component has exactly c - 1 edges, so every component is a tree.

options.text: k = n - m
options.why: This holds only for forests; a cycle adds an edge without merging components.

options.text: Adding any new edge reduces k by exactly 1.
options.why: An edge inside an existing component leaves k unchanged.

questions.solution:
1. Spanning trees of the components use n - k edges, so m >= n - k.
2. Equality means no extra edge: a forest.
3. Extra edges create cycles without changing k.

questions.stem: Which statements about depth-first search are true?

options.text: A directed graph has a cycle if and only if some DFS of it produces a back edge.
options.why: A back edge closes a cycle with tree edges; conversely the first vertex of a cycle to be discovered gets a back edge from the cycle.

options.text: DFS of an undirected graph produces only tree edges and back edges.
options.why: An undirected edge to a finished vertex would have been explored from that vertex first, so forward and cross edges cannot appear.

options.text: For a cross edge u→v, d[v] > d[u].
options.why: A cross edge goes to a vertex discovered and finished earlier: d[v] < f[v] < d[u].

options.text: A DFS of a DAG may produce a back edge if the start vertex is chosen badly.
options.why: A back edge always closes a cycle, so no DFS of a DAG has one.

questions.solution:
1. Back edge <=> cycle (directed).
2. Undirected: only tree and back edges.
3. Cross edge: v already finished, so d[v] < d[u].

options.why: p, then q (s still waits for r), then u frees r and v; r frees s; s before v alphabetically; v frees t.

options.text: p u q r v s t
options.why: Used a FIFO queue in discovery order instead of always taking the smallest available vertex.

options.text: p q r s t u v
options.why: Plain alphabetical order breaks the edge u→r: r cannot come before u.

options.text: u v p r q s t
options.why: This is the DFS reverse-finishing order; it is a valid order but not the one this rule produces.

2. Available {q, u}: take q. Then u -> r, v free.
3. Available {r, v}: r -> s free. Available {s, v}: s. Then v -> t. Order p q u r s v t.

options.why: Gave the finishing order without reversing it; it lists every sink first.

options.text: p q s t r u v
options.why: Gave the discovery (preorder) order; u→r is violated because r appears before u.

options.text: p q u r s v t

questions.stem: Which statements about single-source shortest paths are true?

options.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is correct whenever all edge weights are non-negative.
options.why: With w >= 0 no path through an unextracted vertex can beat the current minimum, so each extracted value is final.

options.text: Bellman-Ford handles negative edges as long as no negative cycle is reachable from the source.
options.why: n - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge cover every simple path.

options.text: Adding the same constant to every edge weight removes negative edges and keeps the shortest paths unchanged.
options.why: A path with k edges gains k·c, so paths with more edges are penalised and the shortest path can change.

options.text: Dijkstra's algorithm works with negative edges provided the graph has no negative cycle.
options.why: No negative cycle is enough for Bellman-Ford, not for Dijkstra; a single negative edge can already break it.

questions.solution:
1. Dijkstra's greedy step needs w >= 0.
2. Bellman-Ford needs only the absence of reachable negative cycles.
3. Reweighting by a constant favours fewer-edge paths; Johnson's method uses vertex potentials instead.
